A drinking glass that performs. Sun Dial takes its name and its logic from the sundial: an instrument that makes time visible not by displaying it, but by translating the position of light into a readable pattern on a surface. The glasses do the same — their engraved walls catch, fragment, and redirect light as the angle of viewing and the level of liquid constantly shift.

Light refraction

The project began with an exploration of the relationship between form, light, and interaction. The starting point was the study of light refraction — not as a decorative effect applied to glass, but as the generative principle behind the form itself.

The process moved from a simple prism, simulating increasingly complex patterns, until surfaces emerged that could fragment, reflect, and modulate light in unexpected ways. Each subsequent variation pushed the engraving logic further, producing effects that change continuously as the user handles the glass.

The prism principle
Every piece in the collection begins from the same optical logic: engraved rectangular elements on the glass surface act as micro-prisms, bending light into spectral colour along their edges while the sandblasted zones diffuse it into soft, directional shadow.
Day and night
The engraved zone — transparent, light-active — corresponds to the sunlit hemisphere of a planisphere. The sandblasted zone — diffuse, matte — corresponds to the night side. The boundary between them traces a curve across the glass surface, modulating with the level of the liquid inside.
False curves
The surface geometry works with fluid curves and dynamic geometries wherever possible, but also exploits "false curves" — broken surfaces and gentle angles that, while maintaining a sharper underlying structure, return a continuous and homogeneous image in reflection. The result is a balance between precision and fluidity.

Form and function

The inspiration for the engraving distribution came from solar projection maps: in planisphere representations, light gradients spread across conical surfaces, marking the passage between the day zone and the night zone with a visual drama that changes with the observer’s position.

This principle was translated directly into the whisky glass. The cylinder becomes a surface capable of modulating light in the same suggestive way, turning the act of drinking into an evolving play of reflections and shadows.

The pattern system

From a small set of primitive elements, a generative engraving system was developed that can produce an entire family of products from a single coherent language. Four base marks — the infinite line, the long line, the rectangle, and the short line — combine into patterns that follow or are bounded by a guiding curve. The position of each element within its row can vary randomly within a defined range, meaning the system could hypothetically generate an unlimited series of unique combinations from an algorithm.

Line (infinite)
A continuous horizontal engraving with no defined endpoints. Used to establish a steady rhythm across the full circumference of the glass, producing even, unbroken light diffusion.
Long line
A bounded horizontal mark, longer than the rectangle. Introduces variation in the light response while maintaining the horizontal register of the overall pattern.
Rectangle
The core element of the system. A 4 × 28 mm engraved rectangle that, when grouped and distributed along the guiding curve, generates the characteristic solar-arc pattern visible across all pieces in the collection.
Short line
The smallest mark. Used at the periphery of patterns to soften the transition between the engraved and sandblasted zones, extending the visual gradient without adding structural weight.

Y2K Futurism

To build a product family with a broader and more autonomous identity, the research moved beyond the solar map concept and pushed toward more expressive formal languages. The reference point was Y2K Futurism — the aesthetic current born between the late 1990s and early 2000s that fused optimistic visions of the future with fluid forms, iridescent colours, and pop references, mixing glamour and space with a hyper-stylistic sensibility.

This reference was interpreted radically but within the constraints of what is actually producible in crystal. Increasingly complex geometries were tested, and the base structure of the glass was varied up to the limit of manufacturing feasibility — generating new light refractions and giving formal identity to an entirely new design language for the collection.

The complete collection

The collection is articulated across six pieces in two macro-categories: a more traditional group tied to recognisable and stable forms, and a more experimental group defined by structural variations that amplify the visual and perceptual effect. All six share the same engraving system and the same day/night surface logic.

No.1 — Daylight 1

The founding piece. A classic whisky tumbler with a circular cross-section and the solar-arc engraving pattern distributed symmetrically across both sides of the glass wall. The sandblasted zones occupy the flanks; the engraved, transparent zone crests at the centre top.

Form
Classic tumbler · circular section
Category
Traditional forms

No.2 — Daylight 2

A second variation on the classic tumbler form. The engraving pattern is adjusted — tighter spacing, subtly different rectangle distribution — producing a denser light effect while the overall silhouette remains identical to No.1. The two pieces are intended to be read as a pair.

Form
Classic tumbler · denser pattern
Category
Traditional forms

No.3 — Daylight 3

The third and final variation in the classic tumbler group. The engraving arc becomes asymmetric, with the pattern distributed more heavily toward one side — introducing a directional quality to the light effect that shifts dramatically as the glass rotates in the hand.

Form
Classic tumbler · asymmetric arc
Category
Traditional forms

No.4 — Pull / Cut 1

The first piece in the experimental category. The tumbler form is pulled and carved at the sides — the wall is hollowed inward at two opposing points, creating an hourglass-like grip zone that also concentrates and intensifies the light refraction effect at those points. In the Cut 1 variant, the top is sheared diagonally, introducing a planar face that reflects light at a fixed angle.

Form
Elongated · side cavities · diagonal cut
Category
Varied forms

No.5 — Globe / Cut 2

The most formally radical piece in the collection. The glass body is spherical — the engraving pattern wraps a convex surface rather than a cylinder, producing a fundamentally different optical behaviour: the light bends around the curve of the globe rather than across it, and the refraction effect becomes omnidirectional. The Cut 2 variant retains the diagonal shear of the opening.

Form
Spherical body · omnidirectional refraction
Category
Varied forms

No.6 — Prism

To intensify reflections and the prism effect, this model replaces the engraved lines with faceted cuts — a new mould-level intervention rather than a surface treatment. The cuts refract light with much greater intensity than wheel-engraving, and the base of the glass is redesigned from scratch to integrate the faceting into the structural form of the piece.

Form
Classic tumbler · faceted cuts · new mould
Category
Varied forms
